species.name: Cobia
specs: During the spring migration anglers find them in roughly 30-70 ft (9-21 m)

Structure-oriented: found near buoys, pilings, platforms, debris, shipwrecks and artificial reefs, and with large animals such as rays, sharks and turtles. Cruise in packs of 3 to 100 during migrations in shallow water along the shore.
Spawns offshore many times through a long season

species.name: Mahi-mahi
specs: Common up to about 50 lb; can reach about 100 lb
Small fish, crabs and shrimp living in sargassum; also flying fish and mackerels
Epipelagic: surface to about 85 m. Satellite-tagged fish spent about 40% of their time within about 1 m of the surface and made occasional dives to about 250 m.
Offshore, drawn to floating structure (sargassum weedlines, flotsam, floating debris). Moves closer to shore in summer as shelf waters warm.
About 6 years; fast growing, matures very young

species.name: Mutton snapper
specs: Common at about 5-15 lb; can reach about 37 in and 30 lb
25-95 m, usually 40-70 m (FishBase); adults deeper than juveniles
Adults live on reefs, ledges and around wrecks and artificial reefs, often patrolling the edge between reef and sand. Juveniles use seagrass and mangroves.

Forms large spawning aggregations on reef promontories along the shelf edge, building the week before the full moon, with spawning 2-5 days after it in the late afternoon. Season is roughly May to August in Florida.

species.name: Atlantic sailfish
specs: Large billfish; anglers target numbers on light tackle rather than size
Mostly the upper 20 m, with repeated short dives to 50-150 m below the thermocline (Gulf of Mexico and Florida Straits tagging)

Stays above the thermocline in about 21-28 C water. In winter along the Florida coast the fish travel just outside the outer reef line, often along the green-to-blue water edge; cold fronts concentrate them.

species.name: Common snook
specs: Up to about 48 in (50 lb) per FWC; Florida state record 45 lb 12 oz
Fish and large crustaceans; pinfish, anchovies and shrimp are major prey in one diet study

Ambush predator that faces moving water and waits for prey to be carried down the current. Uses mangrove shorelines, seagrass, beaches, river mouths, docks and other structure. Retreats to deeper channels, backcountry bays and rivers during cold fronts.

April through October in Florida, with peaks around June to September. Spawning aggregations form at inlets, passes, river mouths and nearshore reefs, with eggs released in the late afternoon and early evening on all tides. Atlantic-coast examples named by FWC include Jupiter and Lake Worth inlets.

species.name: Atlantic tarpon
specs: Adults eat mostly mid-water prey: mullets, pinfish, marine catfishes; crabs are a spring favorite at inlets
Normal habitat to about 30 m; tolerates salinities from fresh to about 47 ppt

Migratory and heat-loving. Adults arrive in the Florida Keys in April once surface water reaches about 26 C, peak in May (26-28 C) and leave in June (27-29 C). Cold fronts push them to warmer, deeper water, and juveniles leave creeks below about 20 C.
April to June in the Florida Keys

species.name: Wahoo
specs: Relatively common at 50-75 lb and can exceed 100 lb
Almost totally fish: mackerels, butterfishes, scads, jacks, flying fish; a little squid
Mostly in the upper mixed layer. Tagging off Baja California found an average depth of about 18 m, with 99% of daytime above the thermocline.
Solitary or in very small loose groups. More common near banks (lumps), drop-offs or weed lines in blue water, along current edges and temperature breaks. Not warm-blooded.

species.name: Yellowtail snapper
specs: Typically 2 to 5 lb and 8 to 14 in; up to about 34 in and 11 lb (NOAA Fisheries). Florida state record 8 lb 9 oz.

Adults mostly 10-70 m over sandy areas near offshore reefs (NOAA Fisheries); commercial handline catch mainly 20-60 m; overall depth range 0-180 m (FishBase). Juveniles use seagrass, mangroves and back reefs.
Reef fish found around coral heads, patch reefs and high-profile artificial structure. Often swarms up a steady chum slick. Juveniles use seagrass and mangrove nursery habitat.
April through August in the southeast U.S. (SAFMC); FishBase notes spawning occurs year-round in parts of the range with different peaks by area
6 to 14 years typical; up to 28 years (NOAA Fisheries)
